VI. BYPASS RESISTANCE FOR ROUTES OF ANY LENGTH

TODO: new heading; the new text of Sec. VI is in the insert after this page. Of the old Sec. VI only the idea of VI-A survives, and it moves to the model section (next note).

TODO: keep this idea, it still holds for csf_final, but move it to Sec. V-A2, right after the paragraph on Forward_HTLC, and drop this heading. Suggested text:

HTLC offers between channel peers are not network messages in our model. With the offer as a public, signed message that each hop forwards, TAMARIN's origin analysis treats every party as a potential sender of a forwarded offer, and for routes of unbounded length the analysis did not terminate. The forward obligation is therefore the private, linear fact Route, which Sender_Offer_HTLC creates and each application of Forward_HTLC consumes and re-creates for the next hop. The price is that the network adversary cannot inject, replay or modify HTLC offers between peers. It still chooses the amounts and the fee of every forward (In(%vIn), In(%fee), In(%vOut)), controls the delivery of the signed invoices, and can compromise any long-term key at any time. A forwarder compromised before its incoming HTLC times out is exempt from T2b and T3, and two compromised parties that have each added an HTLC for the same payment hash can apply AttackerSkip.

inserts.title: NEW Sec. VI: Bypass Resistance for Routes of Any Length (replaces the old Sec. VI)
inserts.html:
VI. BYPASS RESISTANCE FOR ROUTES OF ANY LENGTH

The wormhole of Sec. V-E lets a payment settle while an honest forwarder between two compromised parties is bypassed: its outgoing HTLC is refunded and it earns no fee. We now show that in our model a bypass requires key compromise: for the forwarder at each of the positions 1 to 6 of a route, and, for payments whose hash is offered on a single channel, for a forwarder at any position of a route of any length. Sections VI-A to VI-D concern the main theory lightning.spthy; there is no separate N-hop theory.

A. Bypass requires compromise

The only rule that produces a Fulfilled fact for an HTLC that was not redeemed is AttackerSkip. It requires the two parties at the ends of the skip, ExitAtt and EntryAtt, to be compromised, and it records Skipped(ptrSkip, x); Fulfilled_Source states that every Fulfilled fact used in a settlement stems from an earlier redemption or skip. Every skip follows a compromise (Skipped_Requires_Compromise, Sec. V-E).

A forwarder is bypassed when the payment settles at the sender while the forwarder's own hop is refunded; Intermediary_Timeout_Refund records such a refund as RefundHop(ptrIn, ptrOut, y). For the first and the second forwarder on the sender's route we prove:

lemma First_Hop_Skip_Requires_Compromise [heuristic={lemmas_first}]:
    "All S F1 R pSF Next pOut x #s #f #r.
        SenderSettled(S, F1, R, pSF, x) @ #s
      & HTLCForwarded(F1, S, Next, pSF, pOut, h(x)) @ #f
      & RefundHop(pSF, pOut, h(x)) @ #r
     ==> Ex P #c. LtkCompromised(P) @ #c"
lemma Second_Hop_Skip_Requires_Compromise [heuristic={lemmas_first}]:
    "All S F1 R pSF x F2 p1 Next pOut #s #f1 #f2 #r.
        SenderSettled(S, F1, R, pSF, x) @ #s
      & HTLCForwarded(F1, S, F2, pSF, p1, h(x)) @ #f1
      & HTLCForwarded(F2, F1, Next, p1, pOut, h(x)) @ #f2
      & RefundHop(p1, pOut, h(x)) @ #r
     ==> Ex P #c. LtkCompromised(P) @ #c"

Hop3_Skip_Requires_Compromise to Hop6_Skip_Requires_Compromise state the same for the forwarder at positions 3 to 6, with the route from the sender's channel spelled out as a chain of HTLCForwarded facts. These six theorems and their seven helper lemmas (Forward_Unique_Per_Incoming, SettledHop_From_Forward, No_Settle_And_Refund_Same_Hop, No_Fulfill_On_Forwarded_Incoming, Redeemed_Source, SenderSettled_Uses_Fulfilled, SettledHop_Uses_Outgoing), the 13 hop-bypass lemmas of make verify, are verified in the full model, with all restrictions, and need no assumption on how often a payment hash is offered. In the wormhole trace Wormhole_Fee_Theft_Reachable, Indiana is the second forwarder (F1 = Att1, F2 = Indiana): Alice settles while Indiana's outgoing HTLC is refunded, and Alice, Bob and Indiana are uncompromised. The trace satisfies the premise of Second_Hop_Skip_Requires_Compromise, and the compromise in the conclusion is that of Att1 and Att2, which AttackerSkip requires; the conclusion cannot be dropped.

B. Routes of any length

Each fixed-depth theorem names the route up to the bypassed forwarder and therefore covers one position only. The general theorem quantifies over any forward of the payment hash instead:

lemma Any_Hop_Skip_Requires_Compromise [heuristic={lemmas_first}]:
  all-traces
  "∀ S F1 R pSF x Me Prev Next pIn pOut #s #f #r.
    ((((SenderSettled( S, F1, R, pSF, x ) @ #s) ∧
       (HTLCForwarded( Me, Prev, Next, pIn, pOut, h(x) ) @ #f)) ∧
      (RefundHop( pIn, pOut, h(x) ) @ #r)) ∧
     (∀ A B p #o. (HTLCOffered( A, B, p, h(x) ) @ #o) ⇒ (p = pSF))) ⇒
    (∃ P #c. LtkCompromised( P ) @ #c)"

The last conjunct of the premise is the single-offer premise: every HTLC offered for h(x) is offered on the sender's channel pSF.

C. Proof

The proof is organised in seven helper lemmas, proved in the same run. Forward_Parent: the incoming HTLC of every forward was offered by a sender or forwarded by the previous hop. Root_First: every forward of a payment hash is, or is preceded by, a forward whose incoming HTLC was offered by a sender. Next_Is_Child: if all offers of the hash are on one channel and Prev forwarded an HTLC to Me, every later forward of the hash is Me's forward of that HTLC or comes after it. Hop_Redeem_Propagates: without compromise, if a forwarder's incoming HTLC is redeemed, so is its outgoing one. Sender_Channel_Redeemed: without compromise, if the sender settles, its own channel was redeemed. Route_Redeemed_Gen: without compromise and if all offers of the hash are on one channel, redemption of the incoming HTLC of a forward carries over to the incoming HTLC of every forward of the hash that does not come earlier. Route_Redeemed_No_Compromise combines it with Sender_Channel_Redeemed and Root_First: without compromise and under the single-offer premise, if the sender settles, the incoming HTLC of every forward of the hash is redeemed. Root_First, Next_Is_Child and Route_Redeemed_Gen are proved by induction over traces. The theorem then takes 7 proof steps. Assume no compromise. By Route_Redeemed_No_Compromise, the bypassed forwarder's incoming HTLC pIn is redeemed. By Redeemed_Source, this redemption is either the settlement of a forward from pIn, which Forward_Unique_Per_Incoming, SettledHop_From_Forward and No_Settle_And_Refund_Same_Hop exclude given RefundHop(pIn, pOut, h(x)), or a fulfilment by the receiver, which No_Fulfill_On_Forwarded_Incoming excludes. The proof scripts of Root_First, Next_Is_Child, Route_Redeemed_Gen, Route_Redeemed_No_Compromise and of the theorem are stored in lightning.spthy; the other helpers are proved automatically.

General mode and trace inclusion. The theorem is proved in a separate mode of the same theory, make general (-D=GENERAL -D=NO_IMC -D=NO_OTF -D=NO_RBT -D=NECESSITY), which enables the general lemmas and removes the three liveness restrictions T1 (RedeemBeforeTimeout), T2b (OutgoingTimesOutFirst) and T3 (IntermediaryMustClaim). Removing a restriction only adds traces, so every trace of the full model is a trace of this mode, and an all-traces property proved in this mode also holds in the full model. The run proves the theorem together with all 23 [reuse] lemmas available in this mode (24/24 verified), so no lemma proved under the removed restrictions is reused; ForwardTimeGap, which is derived from T2b, is not a [reuse] lemma in this mode. Bypass resistance for single-offer payments therefore does not depend on T1, T2b or T3.

D. Caveats

  • Single-offer premise. The theorem is proved only for payments whose hash is offered on a single channel. If the same hash is offered on several channels, several routes carry it, and the theorem says nothing about a forwarder on such a payment. The fixed-depth theorems do not need the premise, because they spell out the route from the settling sender's channel; for such payments they cover positions 1 to 6 of that route.
  • Weak conclusion. The conclusion states only that some party's long-term key was compromised at some point of the trace. It does not say which party (for instance a neighbour of the bypassed forwarder, as in the wormhole) and does not order the compromise before the settlement or the refund. The fixed-depth theorems have the same conclusion; only Skipped_Requires_Compromise orders the compromise before the skip.
  • Liveness restrictions. The six fixed-depth theorems are proved in the full model, with T1, T2b and T3 in place, and we have not checked them without these restrictions. For a payment whose hash is offered on several channels, bypass resistance at positions 1 to 6 therefore rests on the liveness restrictions; only Any_Hop_Skip_Requires_Compromise (single-offer payments) is shown to hold without them.

Results. make verify: Skipped_Requires_Compromise and the 13 hop-bypass lemmas verified (full model). make general: 24/24 verified, Any_Hop_Skip_Requires_Compromise in 7 steps.

inserts.title: NEW Sec. VI-E: Countermeasure: PTLC (end of the new Sec. VI)
inserts.html:
E. Countermeasure: PTLC

The wormhole works because every channel of an HTLC route is locked with the same hash h(x): once x is known at one point of the route, a compromised party can use it on a channel further upstream. Malavolta et al. [6] replace the shared lock by anonymous multi-hop locks, the basis of point time-locked contracts (PTLCs): every channel has its own lock, and a forwarder can compute the secret of its incoming lock only from the secret of its outgoing lock and its own tweak, chosen by the sender. We compare both designs in two small models of lightning_aux.spthy that differ only in how the channel secrets are derived and, accordingly, in how an honest hop obtains its incoming secret (Hop_Settle): -D=PTLC (per-hop secrets) and -D=HTLC (one shared secret, the baseline).

Model. Both models fix the route S → H1 → H2 → H3 → R over channels c0, c1, c2, c3. Sender_Setup draws a fresh secret x and per-hop tweaks t1, t2, t3 and derives the channel secrets by a hash chain s_in = h(<s_out, t>): s3 = x, s2 = h(<s3, t3>), s1 = h(<s2, t2>), s0 = h(<s1, t1>); channel ci is locked with h(si). An honest hop that learns the secret of its outgoing channel derives the secret of its incoming channel with its tweak (Hop_Settle). The hash chain is a symbolic stand-in for the additive tweak of PTLCs built from adaptor signatures [6], s_in = s_out + t: in both, deriving a hop's incoming secret requires that hop's tweak. In the HTLC baseline s0 = s1 = s2 = s3 = x, i.e. one hash lock h(x) on every channel, and Hop_Settle passes the outgoing secret on unchanged. The two rules of the PTLC model that implement the per-hop locks:

rule Sender_Setup:
    let s3 = ~x
        s2 = h(<s3, ~t3>)
        s1 = h(<s2, ~t2>)
        s0 = h(<s1, ~t1>)
    in
    [ Fr(~x), Fr(~c0), Fr(~c1), Fr(~c2), Fr(~c3), Fr(~t1), Fr(~t2), Fr(~t3) ]
    --[ Pay($S, $H1, $H2, $H3, $R, ~c0, ~c1, ~c2, ~c3),
        Neq($S, $H1), Neq($S, $H2), Neq($S, $H3), Neq($S, $R),
        Neq($H1, $H2), Neq($H2, $H3), Neq($H1, $H3),
        Neq($H1, $R), Neq($H2, $R), Neq($H3, $R) ]->
    [ !Lock(~c0, $S, $H1, h(s0)), Open(~c0), SenderWait($S, ~c0),
      !Hop($H1, ~c0, ~c1, $H2, h(s1), ~t1),
      !Hop($H2, ~c1, ~c2, $H3, h(s2), ~t2),
      !Hop($H3, ~c2, ~c3, $R,  h(s3), ~t3),
      !RecvSecret($R, ~c3, ~x),
      Out(h(s0)), Out(h(s1)), Out(h(s2)), Out(h(s3)) ]
rule Hop_Settle:
    [ Pend($H, cIn, cOut, t), ClaimInfo(cOut, sec), !Lock(cIn, P, $H, Lin), Open(cIn) ]
    --[ Redeemed(cIn), HopSettled($H, cIn, cOut), Eq(h(h(<sec, t>)), Lin) ]->
    [ ClaimInfo(cIn, h(<sec, t>)), Out(h(<sec, t>)) ]

The adversary is the same in both models: Dolev–Yao plus compromise of any party at any time (rule Compromise). A compromised hop leaks its tweak (Leak_Tweak); every secret used to claim a channel is published, as it would be on chain; a compromised payee may claim its channel with any value the adversary knows and that opens the lock (Adversary_Claim). There is no skip rule: a wormhole has to be built from adversary knowledge alone. Timing is abstracted: an open HTLC may be refunded at any time (Refund).

Results. With per-hop locks, the sender's channel c0 is never redeemed while H2's outgoing channel c2 is refunded, as long as S and H2 are uncompromised, whichever of H1, H3 and R are compromised (all-traces, verified, 25 steps):

lemma No_Wormhole_Around_Honest_Hop:
  all-traces
  "not (
Ex S H1 H2 H3 R c0 c1 c2 c3 #p #a #b.
      Pay(S, H1, H2, H3, R, c0, c1, c2, c3) @ #p
    & Redeemed(c0) @ #a
    & Refunded(c2) @ #b
    & not (Ex #k. Compromised(H2) @ #k)
    & not (Ex #k. Compromised(S) @ #k))"

With the shared hash lock, the same situation is reachable (exists-trace, verified, 12 steps):

lemma Wormhole_Around_Honest_Hop:
  exists-trace
  "Ex S H1 H2 H3 R c0 c1 c2 c3 #p #a #b.
      Pay(S, H1, H2, H3, R, c0, c1, c2, c3) @ #p
    & Redeemed(c0) @ #a
    & Refunded(c2) @ #b
    & not (Ex #k. Compromised(H2) @ #k)
    & not (Ex #k. Compromised(S) @ #k)"

Two control lemmas show that the PTLC result is not vacuous. Control_Refund_Of_H2_Outgoing (exists-trace, 6 steps): H2's outgoing HTLC can be refunded while H2 is honest, so the refund in the premise is not excluded by the model itself. Control_Wormhole_If_H2_Compromised (exists-trace, 18 steps): once H2 itself is compromised, the bypass is reachable with S still uncompromised, so the safety proof depends on H2 being honest.

lemma Control_Refund_Of_H2_Outgoing:
  exists-trace
  "Ex S H1 H2 H3 R c0 c1 c2 c3 #p #b.
      Pay(S, H1, H2, H3, R, c0, c1, c2, c3) @ #p
    & Refunded(c2) @ #b
    & not (Ex #k. Compromised(H2) @ #k)"
lemma Control_Wormhole_If_H2_Compromised:
  exists-trace
  "Ex S H1 H2 H3 R c0 c1 c2 c3 #p #a #b #k.
      Pay(S, H1, H2, H3, R, c0, c1, c2, c3) @ #p
    & Redeemed(c0) @ #a
    & Refunded(c2) @ #b
    & Compromised(H2) @ #k
    & not (Ex #j. Compromised(S) @ #j)"

Sanity lemmas in both models show that a payment completes end to end without any compromise (Honest_Payment_Completes: 10 steps in PTLC, 10 in HTLC) and with both neighbours H1 and H3 of H2 compromised (Colluders_Present_Payment_Completes: 14 steps in PTLC, 8 in HTLC). All eight lemmas are verified by make aux (PTLC 5/5, HTLC 3/3).

Limitations. The two models are separate from lightning.spthy: a fixed route with three intermediaries and one honest hop under attack, no channel layer, abstract timing, and an honest Sender_Setup that chooses all locks and tweaks consistently. The hash chain abstracts the group operation of the adaptor-signature construction: it captures that a hop's incoming secret requires that hop's tweak, but not the algebra of [6] (an XOR encoding exhausted memory in TAMARIN). We therefore claim the contrast between the two lock designs on this route, not a PTLC result for routes of any length.

inserts.title: Sec. VII Related Work: rewritten body + new reference
inserts.html:
VII. RELATED WORK

Grundmann and Hartenstein [8] model-check a stepwise refinement of the Lightning Network in TLA+; model checking explores a bounded state space. Our TAMARIN proofs are symbolic and unbounded: subject to the restrictions of our model (Sec. IV-A), including three liveness restrictions, they cover any number of parties, channels, channel updates and payments, and, for bypass resistance of single-offer payments (Sec. VI), routes of any length. [9] presents a formally verified Lightning Network. TODO: one sentence on the scope and the tool of [9] and how it differs from our work.

Kiayias and Litos [24] give a composable security treatment of the Lightning Network: they define an ideal functionality for a payment network and prove, in the universal composability framework, that the Lightning protocol realises it. Their guarantee is computational and composable, and their proof is by hand. Ours are symbolic but machine-checked by TAMARIN; they include bypass resistance for routes of any length (for single-offer payments), and they contrast the wormhole under HTLCs with its absence under PTLC-style locks on a fixed route.

Malavolta et al. [6] describe the wormhole attack on HTLC-based multi-hop payments and propose anonymous multi-hop locks as a countermeasure; their instantiation with adaptor signatures is the basis of PTLCs. Our main model reproduces the wormhole (Wormhole_Fee_Theft_Reachable, Sec. V-E), and our auxiliary models check the countermeasure symbolically on a fixed route (Sec. VI-E).

Smith et al. [22] formalise agent-skipping attacks on message-forwarding protocols; the wormhole is an instance of such an attack. Our bypass theorems (Sec. VI) state the corresponding security property for Lightning routing: a forwarder at positions 1 to 6 of a route, or at any position for single-offer payments, can be skipped only if some long-term key is compromised.

New reference (TODO: add to the reference list, same entry as in the note on p. 13; numbered by first citation, after Backes et al. [23], who are cited in the liveness-scope paragraph added after p. 11):

[24] A. Kiayias and O. S. T. Litos, “A Composable Security Treatment of the Lightning Network,” in 2020 IEEE 33rd Computer Security Foundations Symposium (CSF), 2020.

inserts.title: NEW Sec. VIII: Limitations (after Related Work, before the conclusion)
inserts.html:
VIII. LIMITATIONS

  • Single-offer premise. The any-length theorem assumes that every HTLC for the payment hash is offered on the sender's channel; when a hash is offered more than once, only the fixed-depth theorems (positions 1 to 6) apply, and these are proved under the liveness restrictions T1, T2b and T3. Its conclusion says that some long-term key was compromised, not whose or when.
  • No end-to-end amounts. Each Forward_HTLC reads its incoming amount, fee and outgoing amount from the network and enforces Eq(%vIn, %vOut %+ %fee), but the offer, the invoice and the Route fact carry no amount. Amounts are therefore not chained along the path, and we make no end-to-end claims about value, e.g. that the receiver obtains the invoiced amount or that the sender pays exactly the path fees.
  • HTLCs are not part of the commitment transactions. The channel layer and the routing layer share the theory, the adversary and the channel topology (HTLCs are added only on opened channels, HTLC_On_Opened_Channel), but HTLC outputs are not folded into the commitment states, and settling or refunding an HTLC does not update the channel state. The coupling that each HTLC is resolved at most once is assumed as the restriction OneResolutionPerHTLC, not derived from the channel layer; we do not claim a composition theorem. A channel carries at most one pending HTLC at a time (Mutex(ptr)).
  • Routing abstraction. HTLC offers travel as the private linear fact Route, not as network messages, so the network adversary cannot inject, replay or modify offers between peers; it chooses amounts and fees, controls the delivery of invoices and can compromise keys. The adversary never learns a preimage (Preimage_Never_Known), so in the main model the wormhole comes from the explicit rule AttackerSkip, which requires the parties at both ends of the skip to be compromised, rather than from adversary knowledge. (The auxiliary PTLC and HTLC models have no such rule.)
  • No onion routing, no privacy. Every forwarder knows its predecessor, its successor and the payment hash, and the next hop is any party with which the forwarder shares a channel. We make no privacy claims.
  • Abstract timing. The main model has no clock: Open_Timeout lets a channel time out at any point allowed by the restrictions, and the restrictions T1, T2b and T3 (the last two only for forwarders not compromised before their incoming HTLC times out) stand in for CLTV deadlines. As restrictions, they remove every trace that violates them, including traces in which an uncompromised forwarder could not have claimed in time; results proved under them say nothing about such runs (only the any-length bypass theorem is proved without them). Concrete block heights appear only in the auxiliary CLOCK and CLTV models.
  • PTLC model. The countermeasure is checked only on the fixed route S → H1 → H2 → H3 → R, with honest lock set-up and a hash chain in place of the adaptor-signature algebra (Sec. VI-E).

ARTIFACT AVAILABILITY

The artifact consists of lightning.spthy (main model: channel layer, multi-hop routing and the wormhole; 37 rules), lightning_aux.spthy (five auxiliary models, selected by -D=PTLC, -D=HTLC, -D=CLOCK, -D=CLTV and -D=TIMEOUT) and a Makefile. make all runs, in this order, make verify (lightning.spthy, full model: 55/55 lemmas verified), make general (Sec. VI: 24/24), make aux (lightning_aux.spthy: 21/21) and make necessity (Sec. V-D); Table I lists what each target proves. All results were obtained with TAMARIN 1.10 and reproduced on a laptop with a 6 GB heap (MEM=6G); make verify-one proves one lemma per run for machines with less memory. TAMARIN 1.10 reports the Maude version used, 3.2, as unsupported; all results above were obtained with it. Every run also reports that TAMARIN's derivation checks, part of its well-formedness checks of the model, timed out; this warning does not concern the proofs.
